sources.citation: Lloyd T, Conti S, Santos F, Steventon A. Effect on secondary care of providing enhanced support to residential and nursing home residents: a subgroup analysis of a retrospective matched cohort study. BMJ Qual Saf. 2019;28(7):534-46.
sources.design: Retrospective matched cohort (linked care home and hospital data)

sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction notice

sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction notice
sources.quality_note: NIHR-funded; evidence mostly low quality per authors.

sources.citation: Shah SM, Carey IM, Harris T, DeWilde S, Cook DG. Mortality in older care home residents in England and Wales. Age Ageing. 2013;42(2):209-15.
sources.design: Cohort study, THIN primary care database
sources.population_setting: 9,772 care home and 354,306 community residents aged 65-104, 293 practices in England and Wales, 2009
sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction notice
sources.quality_note: Prevalent residents (not new admissions), one year of follow-up, 2009 data; describes residents in a home at a point in time, not survival from the date of moving in.

claims.claim: 'Potentially avoidable' (ambulatory care sensitive) admissions are defined by lists of diagnosis codes, and the lists vary, which changes how many admissions are counted as avoidable.
claims.supporting_passage: The underlying ICD10 codes used to define ACSCs vary widely across subsets of ACSCs used in the NHS. This impacts on rates of admission, length of stay and costs attributable to ACSCs. ... different conceptual interpretations of the term 'ACSC' and use of differing definitions and diagnostic codes impact on the proportion of admissions that are attributed as ACSCs.
claims.pico_timeframe: All emergency admissions, England 2005/6; comparison of ACSC definitions (36 vs NHS subset of 19 conditions)
claims.safe_wording: 'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes. Different lists give different totals.
claims.qualifications: Study was of all emergency admissions, not care homes; it shows the classification is code-based, it does not itself state 'no case review' for any specific report.

numbers.meaning: NHS subset of ACSCs used 19 of 36 conditions found in the literature
share of ACSC admissions (36-condition set) attributable to NHS 19-condition subset, England 2005/6

claims.claim: The measure is used to judge services: 'potentially avoidable emergency admissions' is an outcome in evaluations of support to care homes.
claims.supporting_passage: Residents of participating residential care homes showed lower rates of potentially avoidable emergency admissions (rate ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.82), emergency admissions (rate ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.86) and Accident & Emergency attendances (0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.81) than matched controls.
claims.pico_timeframe: People 65+ moving into Rushcliffe care homes 2014-16 with enhanced support vs matched controls
claims.safe_wording: Rates of 'potentially avoidable' admissions are used to compare services and programmes for care homes.
claims.qualifications: Use only to show how the measure is used; do not quote the rate ratio as the post's point. Observational.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No difference was found for nursing home residents.

claims.claim: Hospital admission from a care home is often necessary; blanket do-not-hospitalise approaches were problematic.
claims.supporting_passage: While often necessary, such admissions can be distressing and provide an opportunity cost as well as a financial cost. ... Advance care planning was key to the success of most quality improvement programmes but do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.
claims.pico_timeframe: Systematic review of interventions to reduce unplanned admissions of care home residents
claims.safe_wording: A 2023 systematic review noted that admissions from care homes are often necessary, and that do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.
claims.qualifications: 'Often necessary' is the authors' framing in the background, not a measured finding.

claims.claim: Wolters et al. 2019 (Health Foundation): about 41 in 100 emergency admissions from care homes were potentially avoidable.
claims.qualifications: No opened copy found in PubMed or Drive; per editor guidance, omit the figure.

claims.claim: About 1 in 4 older care home residents died within one year; mortality was higher in nursing homes than residential homes, relative to the general population of the same age and sex.
claims.supporting_passage: a total of 2,558 (26.2%) care home and 11,602 (3.3%) community residents died within 1 year. The age and sex standardised mortality ratio for nursing homes was 419 (95% CI: 396-442) and for residential homes was 284 (266-302).
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents aged 65-104 in care homes vs community, England and Wales, 2009, 1-year follow-up
claims.safe_wording: In a study of care home residents in England and Wales in 2009, about 26 in 100 died within a year, so about 74 in 100 were alive a year later. Death rates were higher in nursing homes than in residential homes.
claims.qualifications: People already living in homes, not people counted from the day they moved in; 2009 data. Higher mortality reflects how ill people are when they move in, not an effect of the home.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No verified UK distribution of survival from admission (median, spread) was found; Forder and Fernandez 2011 was not opened.

numbers.meaning: care home residents 65+ who died within 1 year, 2009, absolute
community residents 65+ who died within 1 year, absolute, not age-matched
age-sex standardised mortality ratio, nursing vs residential homes (population = 100)

claims.claim: A median is the value that half the group exceeds.
claims.safe_wording: A median survival means half the group lived longer than that figure and half lived less.
claims.qualifications: Standard statistical definition; no source needed.

claims.claim: Median length of stay in UK care homes, with spread from weeks to years (Forder and Fernandez 2011).
claims.safe_wording: Do not give a median length of stay or a histogram.
claims.qualifications: PSSRU report not indexed or opened.

claims.claim: Enhanced Health in Care Homes alignment and weekly home round; Scottish My Health My Care My Home; CQC Smiling Matters.
claims.qualifications: All are official web documents that cannot be opened; not searched further because C16-06 is a reserve and not needed (C16-12 is revise, not drop).

candidates.reason: Core point (diagnosis-code classification, used as a planning/comparison measure, admission often necessary) supported by PubMed-indexed papers. The Wolters proportion is not available and must be omitted.
No verified UK median/spread of survival from admission. Shah 2013 supports a one-year figure and a nursing vs residential difference.
candidates.revised_angle: Use Shah 2013: about 26 in 100 care home residents in England and Wales died within a year (2009), so about 74 in 100 were alive a year later; nursing homes had higher death rates than residential homes. Explain that a group figure (and any median) cannot tell a family about one person, that higher mortality reflects how ill people are when they move in, and end on asking the clinician what they expect for this person. No length-of-stay histogram; illustrative icon strip must be labelled illustrative.

candidates.reason: Essential service claims rest on NHS England, Scottish Government and CQC web documents that could not be opened; not needed as fallback since C16-12 is revise.
